2) Allergic contact dermatitis — very likely within the spongiotic spectrum. Rationale: adult-onset, chronic course and biopsy appearance are compatible; often localized and progressive with ongoing exposure.  
3) Psoriasis vulgaris (chronic plaque psoriasis) — possible. Rationale: psoriasiform hyperplasia on biopsy supports psoriasis, but concurrent spongiosis is less typical, making psoriasis less favored than spongiotic dermatitis.  
4) Dermatophyte infection (tinea corporis) — less likely but important to exclude. Rationale: can produce psoriasiform changes and clinical mimicry; requires fungal testing.  
5) Seborrheic dermatitis / other spongiotic dermatitis variants — alternative consideration. Rationale: overlap in histology and clinical presentation with chronic spongiotic eczema.

- Focused skin exam to document lesion morphology, distribution, scale, and presence/absence of mucosal involvement.  
- KOH scraping +/- fungal culture of an active border to exclude tinea.  
- Patch testing if contact dermatitis suspected (history or distribution suggests contact).  
- Therapeutic trial (short course topical mid‑potency corticosteroid) and response assessment.  
- Medication review and full exposure history.
